extracted.intended_audience: inventors and technology creators (e.g., university faculty, staff, and students) seeking to perform a basic prior art search
extracted.subtask_description: Step‑by‑step practical guidance for inventors to search for existing patents and patent applications (prior art) to assess novelty and non‑obviousness of an invention. Emphasizes using public patent databases, keyword strategies, skimming, and detailed reading of relevant documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology may be patented if the invention is new, useful and non-obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prior art (the body of knowledge existing prior to the invention) to determine whether the invention meets 'new' and 'non-obvious' requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and distinguish prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'prior art' (i.e., the body of knowledge existing prior to the invention) helps determine whether or not the invention is 'new' and 'non-obvious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is important to know and understand the prior art so that one can make distinctions between the prior art (what is already known) and the invention (what is new).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple patent search platforms (web)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors can perform basic prior art searches to see what knowledge (usually in the form of patents) already exist in the invention's scientific area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can utilize Google Patents or the World Intellectual Property Organization's IP Portal search to perform searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access public patent databases (Delphion, USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accessing a publicly available patent database is a core step in a basic patent search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Delphion patent database is user-friendly and online; there you can view the first pages of patents. For full text views please email OTL (they can download PDF versions). The USPTO website is another reasonably user-friendly patent database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform keyword-based searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing a search based on keywords that would logically be within a summary statement of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use Delphion, click 'Advanced Search' and insert your first keyword or combination of keywords. Then check the boxes for every type of patent (since you're trying to find all existing patents that contain that keyword). Repeat this step for various combinations of keywords until you think you've found the relevant existing patents and patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skim initial patent pages to triage results
rubrics_metrics.description: Skimming the first pages of each patent or patent application to eliminate irrelevant records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By skimming the first pages of each patent or patent application you can eliminate a majority of the records from your search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read relevant patents/applications in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you've re-read the patent applications that seem relevant to your technology, examine them thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After detailed review of key patents/applications, contact OTL to discuss findings or to gain access to PDF versions of the key patents that your search uncovered (contact information provided).
